section.title: The Way, the Truth, and the Life
section.sectionRationale: With His departure looming, Jesus comforts His troubled disciples. He is going to prepare a place in the Father's house and will come again for them. To Thomas He gives the sixth I am saying, I am the way and the truth and the life, and to Philip He reveals that to see Him is to see the Father. He promises the coming of the Spirit, the Advocate, and leaves His peace, so that even His going is for their good.
section.thesis: Jesus calms His disciples' fear by promising to prepare a place for them and to come again, revealing Himself as the only way to the Father and the perfect image of the Father, and pledging the gift of the Spirit and His own peace, so that His departure is not abandonment but the path to a deeper union with the Father and the Son.
section.frameNote: Four movements: comfort in the promise of the Father's house and Jesus' return; the way, the truth, and the life, and the vision of the Father in the Son; the promise of the Spirit and the indwelling of the Father and the Son; and the gift of peace against a troubled heart.

units.label: The Father's house
units.note: I go to prepare a place for you

verses.text: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well.
In My Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you?
And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am.
You know the way to the place where I am going.”

units.label: The way, the truth, and the life
units.note: anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father

verses.text: “Lord,” said Thomas, “we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?”
Jesus answered, “{{egoeimi|I am}} the {{hodos|way}} and the {{aletheia|truth}} and the {{zoe|life}}. No one comes to the Father except through Me.
If you had known Me, you would know My Father as well. From now on you do know Him and have seen Him.”
Philip said to Him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.”
Jesus replied, “Philip, I have been with you all this time, and still you do not know Me? Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?
Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me? The words I say to you, I do not speak on My own. Instead, it is the Father dwelling in Me, performing His works.
Believe Me that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me, or at least believe on account of the works themselves.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes in Me will also do the works that I am doing. He will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father.
And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it.

units.label: The promise of the Spirit
units.note: another Advocate to be with you forever

verses.text: If you love Me, you will keep My commandments.
And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another {{parakletos|Advocate}} to be with you forever,
the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive Him, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him, for He abides with you and will be in you.
I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.
In a little while the world will see Me no more, but you will see Me. Because I live, you also will live.
On that day you will know that I am in My Father, and you are in Me, and I am in you.
Whoever has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me. The one who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and reveal Myself to him.”
Judas (not Iscariot) asked Him, “Lord, why are You going to reveal Yourself to us and not to the world?”
Jesus replied, “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him.
Whoever does not love Me does not keep My words. The word that you hear is not My own, but it is from the Father who sent Me.
All this I have spoken to you while I am still with you.
But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you.
Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid.
You heard Me say, ‘I am going away, and I am coming back to you.’ If you loved Me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.
And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it does happen, you will believe.
I will not speak with you much longer, for the prince of this world is coming, and he has no claim on Me.
But I do exactly what the Father has commanded Me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Get up! Let us go on from here.

egoeimi.gloss: I am. In the sixth great I am saying Jesus declares, I am the way and the truth and the life. As with the other sayings, the phrase names both a rich reality and the divine self. Jesus is not merely a signpost to the Father but the way itself, and no one comes to the Father except through Him.

hodos.gloss: Way, road, path. To Thomas's question about the way, Jesus answers that He is the way, the sole road to the Father. Early believers were even called followers of the Way. The truth and the life are bound to it: He is the way because He is the truth revealed and the life given, so that coming to the Father runs only through Him.

aletheia.gloss: Truth, reality as God defines it. Jesus is the truth in person, the full and reliable revelation of God, so that to know Him is to know the Father. His truth is not abstract doctrine but a person to be trusted and followed, the one in whom the Father is truly seen.

zoe.gloss: Life, the life of God, eternal life. Jesus is the life, its source and giver; because He lives, His people will live. The way, the truth, and the life together declare that Jesus is the only path to the Father, the true revelation of Him, and the life that union with Him brings.

parakletos.gloss: Advocate, Comforter, Helper, Counselor, one called alongside. Jesus promises another Advocate, the Holy Spirit, of the same kind as Himself, to be with the disciples forever. The Spirit continues Jesus' presence with them, teaching, reminding, and dwelling within, so that His departure gives way to an even closer indwelling of God.

basic.context: The disciples are shaken by Jesus' talk of leaving. He tells them not to be troubled: He is going to His Father's house to prepare a place for them, and He will come back for them. When Thomas asks how they can know the way, Jesus says, I am the way and the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through Me. When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus says that to see Him is to see the Father. He then promises the Holy Spirit, another Advocate who will be with them forever and live in them, and He leaves them His peace, so their hearts need not be afraid.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter is pastoral comfort grounded in who Jesus is. The key questions are, how can we come to the Father, and how will we cope when Jesus is gone. Jesus answers that He alone is the way to the Father, that seeing Him is seeing the Father, and that His going will bring the Spirit and a deeper indwelling of God. The exclusivity of verse 6 is not narrow bigotry but the good news that the only way to God has been opened for all in Christ. Love for Jesus shows itself in keeping His word.
basic.originalLanguages: The heart of the chapter is the sixth I am saying: ego eimi, I am the hodos, the way, and the aletheia, the truth, and the zoe, the life. And Jesus promises another parakletos, Advocate, the Spirit who will be with and in His people forever.
basic.typology: The Father's house with many rooms fulfills the longing for God's dwelling with His people. The way to the Father, once guarded since Eden, is opened in Christ. The promised Spirit fulfills the prophets' hope of God's Spirit poured out and dwelling within.
basic.christ: Christ is the way, the truth, and the life, the only access to the Father and His perfect image. He is one with the Father, dwelling in Him and He in the Son. He goes to prepare a place, sends the Spirit, and gives a peace the world cannot give.
basic.god: God is the Father whose house has room for many, who is seen in the Son, who sends the Spirit in the Son's name, and who, with the Son, comes to make His home in those who love Him. The triune God is unveiled in this chapter.
basic.crossReferences: John 1 said the Son makes the Father known. Ephesians 2 speaks of access to the Father through Christ. Romans 8 describes the Spirit's indwelling. Ezekiel 36 promised God's Spirit within His people.
basic.oneStory: The way back to the Father, closed since the garden, is reopened in Jesus, the way, the truth, and the life. He goes ahead to prepare a place and sends the Spirit so that the triune God comes to dwell with His people, bringing a peace the troubled world cannot give and a hope of being forever where He is.

context.literary:
John 14 is the first movement of the Farewell Discourse and works as a question and answer session. Each time Jesus makes a promise, a disciple interrupts with a puzzled question. Thomas asks about the road in verse 5, Philip asks to be shown the Father in verse 8, and Judas, not Iscariot, asks why Jesus will show Himself to them and not to the world in verse 22. Each question exposes how little the disciples have grasped, and each answer carries the argument forward. The chapter is shaped by the disciples' confusion as much as by Jesus' teaching.

The chapter is bracketed by the same command. 'Do not let your hearts be troubled' stands in verse 1 and returns in verse 27, with 'do not be afraid' added. Between them the comfort is laid out in three stages. The first is a place and a return, verses 1 to 4. The second is a person who reveals the Father, verses 5 to 14. The third is a presence who remains, verses 15 to 26. The word 'troubled' is the one John has used of Jesus Himself at Lazarus's tomb, 11:33, in the face of the cross, 12:27, and at the table, 13:21. He asks them to be calm in the very place where He was not.

Two strands run through the whole chapter and are tied together. One is keeping and loving. The chain 'if you love Me, you will keep My commandments' in verse 15 returns in verses 21 and 23 and again in verse 24. The other is the language of dwelling and coming: the many rooms in verse 2, the Spirit who 'abides with you' in verse 17, and the Father and Son who 'will come to him and make Our home with him' in verse 23. The promise of a home in the Father's house and the promise of a home made in the believer are the same promise heard from two ends.

The last verse is abrupt: 'Get up! Let us go on from here.' Yet the discourse continues for three more chapters. Some readers see a seam where two versions of the discourse were joined, and others see a pause in which the little company stands and Jesus keeps speaking on the way. Either way, chapter 14 stands as a unit, a complete consolation, before the more demanding teaching of chapters 15 and 16 begins.
context.historical:
The scene is the upper room on the night before the crucifixion. Jesus has just told Peter that he cannot follow now, 13:36, and has announced a betrayal. The disciples face the loss of the one on whom they staked their lives. In that setting the sentence 'I am going there to prepare a place for you' is not a theological abstraction but a plea to stay calm while everything they trusted slipped away.

'My Father's house' would have sounded familiar to anyone who had heard Jesus call the temple by that title in John 2:16. The temple in Jerusalem was the place where God dwelt among His people, and now Jesus speaks of a house with many rooms and of Himself as the one who prepares the way into it. Some interpreters link the picture to the custom of a bridegroom adding a room to his father's house before returning for his bride. The text never uses the image of a wedding here, so it is better held as a possible echo than as the point.

When Jesus calls Himself 'the way,' the phrase would have recalled how Israel spoke of the right life. 'Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth,' prays the psalmist, Psalm 86:11, and Isaiah called for a highway for God in the wilderness, Isaiah 40:3. The community at Qumran applied Isaiah's words about the way in the wilderness to itself, and the first Christians were called people of 'the Way,' Acts 9:2. The title was in the air. Jesus claims that He is not one who points down the road but the road.

Philip's request to be shown the Father reflects a deep Israelite longing. Moses had asked to see God's glory, Exodus 33:18, and the Law taught that no one could see God and live. Thomas and Philip are not being foolish. They are asking the question every devout Israelite had asked, and Jesus tells them that it has been answered in the one they had walked beside. The peace He leaves, 'not as the world gives,' is the Hebrew shalom, a peace of wholeness and not just quiet, and it stands against the peace of a world order secured by force.
context.canonical:
The chapter gathers up three Old Testament longings and answers each. The first is the longing for a home with God. God had said to Israel, 'they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them,' Exodus 25:8, and promised through Ezekiel 'My dwelling place will be with them,' Ezekiel 37:27. John 14 speaks of a house and a dwelling, and Revelation 21:3 announces that 'the dwelling place of God is with man.' The second is the longing for access. The way to the tree of life was closed at Eden with cherubim and a flaming sword, Genesis 3:24, and the way to the Most Holy Place was closed by a curtain, but Hebrews 10:19 and 20 says Jesus opened 'a new and living way' through the curtain of His body.

The third is the longing for the Spirit. Ezekiel 36:27 and 37:14 promised that God would put His Spirit within His people, and Joel 2:28 said He would pour it out on all people. John 7:39 explains that the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified, and Acts 2:33 reports that the exalted Jesus received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured it out. Romans 8:9 to 11 and Galatians 4:6 describe the Spirit as the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of the Son who lives in believers and lets them cry 'Abba, Father.'

The claims about the Son's relation to the Father are echoed in the rest of the New Testament. Colossians 1:15 calls Him 'the image of the invisible God,' Hebrews 1:3 the 'exact representation of His nature,' and Colossians 2:9 says the fullness of the Deity dwells in Him bodily. Acts 4:12 states the exclusive claim in the apostles' own preaching, 'there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved,' and Ephesians 2:18 gives the Trinitarian shape of access, 'through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wrote for a community that had seen Jesus leave and was not sure what that meant. The discourse tells them that His absence is not a loss, because the Father's house, the Son's return and the Spirit's coming are all in motion. He wants the readers to hear that they have not been left to themselves and that the one they believe in is the same one who stood with the first disciples in that room.

He also wants them to see that the knowledge of God is not a private mystery for the few. When Philip asks to see the Father, he is told he has been seeing Him all along. The author presses the claim that God has made Himself known in a person, and that no mystic path, rival teacher or new revelation needs to be added. This gave the church a firm answer to those who offered other ways to God.

The chapter is also written to form love. The repeated link between love and keeping His word means that the reader is not asked for sentiment alone. John closes the loop between relationship and obedience, and he wants his readers to know that the one who loves Jesus will find the Father and the Son coming to make a home in them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is promise, not command. Jesus describes what He will do, preparing a place, coming back, sending the Spirit, giving peace, and it would be a mistake to turn these promises into duties. The commands that do appear are few and plain: do not let your hearts be troubled, believe, keep My word. These follow from the promises and are meant to be lived in their light.

Two verses need care. The promise of 'greater things' in verse 12 and the promise to do 'whatever you ask in My name' in verses 13 and 14 were spoken to the Eleven in the upper room, and they are not a blank cheque. Asking in His name means asking in line with His character and for the Father's glory, as the end of verse 13 says. And the exclusive claim of verse 6 is a statement about who Jesus is and what He has done, not a licence for contempt toward those who do not yet believe. The same Jesus who says it is the one who will lay down His life for them.

debates.question: What are the 'greater works' of verse 12?

views.label: Greater in extent
views.case: Jesus' ministry was confined to a small region and a few years. After His going to the Father the gospel spread to the nations, and the disciples' works are greater in reach and number. Acts 2:41 reports three thousand added in a day, which no earlier day of Jesus' ministry records.

views.label: Greater in kind, because of the Spirit
views.case: The works are made possible 'because I am going to the Father,' that is, because the Spirit is poured out. The disciples now bring people to new birth, John 3:5 to 8, and proclaim a finished work, which the disciples could not do before the cross. The greatness is that of the new age, not of individual power.

views.label: Greater signs of power
views.case: Some take the promise as a pledge of miracles beyond those Jesus performed. The text does not say this, and the works He describes in the context, verses 10 and 11, are the works of the Father in the Son, so the works of the disciples are works of the same Father through them.

debates.bearing: All views agree on the cause. The works are done by those who believe in Him, because He has gone to the Father and the Spirit is given. The disciples do not become greater than the Lord. The Lord multiplies His work through them.

debates.question: Is the exclusive claim of verse 6 fair?

views.label: Yes, it is the plain meaning and good news
views.case: Jesus says no one comes to the Father except through Him, and Acts 4:12 repeats the claim. The claim is made by the one who says He is the truth, and it is offered to all. The way is open to everyone because He is the way, and not because anyone has found it.

views.label: It is inclusive in its offer, though narrow in its means
views.case: Some stress that the passage says how people come to the Father, not who may be saved from among those who have not heard. They hold that Christ's work is the only ground of salvation while leaving open how God applies it. Others reply that the New Testament consistently ties salvation to hearing and believing the gospel, Romans 10:14 and 15.

views.label: It is a confession of the community, not a universal law
views.case: A few scholars take the sentence as the language of a persecuted community speaking of its own devotion. This reading has to set aside the plain grammar of the verse and the 'no one' and 'except' that frame it.

debates.bearing: The verse should be read slowly and humbly. It is a claim about Jesus, offered in love to a frightened friend, and it is meant to be good news for everyone who is lost and needs a way.

debates.question: Where and when does Jesus 'come back' in verse 3?

views.label: At the end of the age
views.case: The 'coming back' to welcome His people into His presence is the Second Coming, as in 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and 17, 'we will always be with the Lord,' and in Matthew 24:30 and 31. The rooms are the place in the Father's presence prepared for the redeemed.

views.label: In the resurrection and the Spirit
views.case: Later in the chapter Jesus says 'I will come to you,' verse 18, and 'in a little while the world will see Me no more, but you will see Me,' verse 19. These seem to describe the resurrection appearances and the Spirit's coming. On this reading the house is the new fellowship in which the Father and Son make their home, verse 23.

views.label: Both, as stages of one coming
views.case: Jesus returns in the Spirit now, and in person at the end. The word for the 'rooms' in verse 2 and the word for the 'home' in verse 23 are the same noun, so the future house and the present indwelling belong together.

debates.bearing: The third view fits the unity of the chapter best. The believer is already a place where the Father and the Son make their home, and will one day be welcomed into the full presence of God.

study.originalLanguages:
In verse 2 the 'rooms' are monai, from the verb meno, to remain or abide. In verse 23 Jesus says that He and the Father 'will come to him and make Our home with him,' monen poiesometha, using the same noun. John uses it in only those two places in his Gospel. The play of language is deliberate: the dwelling places that Jesus prepares in the Father's house are matched by the dwelling that the Father and Son make in the believer. The two promises are one promise, seen from the two ends of the believer's story.

Verse 1 holds an ambiguity that Greek leaves open. The word pisteuete can be read as an indicative, 'you believe,' or as an imperative, 'believe,' and it stands twice in the same sentence. The BSB takes the first as a statement and the second as a command, but 'believe in God and believe in Me' is also possible. All the readings make the same demand. Jesus is asking that trust in God extend to trust in Him.

The three nouns of verse 6 each carry an article, 'the way, the truth and the life,' and each is a title the Old Testament would have prepared the reader for. The hodos, way, recalls the path of the LORD in Psalm 86:11. The aletheia, truth, is the faithfulness and reliability of God, and the reader would hear the same word in verse 17 when the Spirit is called 'the Spirit of truth.' The zoe, life, is the life of God Himself, which in John 11:25 Jesus claims to be. Many readers take the way as the main claim and the truth and life as its explanation, since He is the way because He is the truth of God and the life of God.

The word 'Advocate' in verses 16 and 26 is parakletos, from para, 'alongside,' and kaleo, 'to call,' meaning someone called to one's side to help, plead or defend. Jesus says 'another Advocate,' using allos, which means another of the same kind, not heteros, another of a different kind. The Spirit is therefore like Jesus in His role, and 1 John 2:1 calls Jesus Himself our advocate with the Father. Jesus adds that the Spirit 'abides with you and will be in you,' verse 17. Some manuscripts read 'is in you' where others read 'will be,' and both readings fit the movement from His presence with the disciples to His presence within them after Easter.

Two further details repay attention. The disciples are promised that they will not be left 'as orphans,' orphanous, verse 18, a word used of children left without a father, which pictures the little band as the family of a departing teacher. And Jesus says of the ruler of this world that 'he has no claim on Me,' verse 30, literally that he 'has nothing in Me,' meaning there is nothing in Jesus on which the ruler can take hold. The pattern is that the sinless one goes to the cross not because the enemy has any right over Him but because He chooses to obey the Father, verse 31.

typology.type: The tabernacle and temple, the house where God dwells
typology.fulfillment: God commanded Israel to make a sanctuary so that He might dwell among them, Exodus 25:8, and Solomon wondered whether even the highest heaven could contain Him, 1 Kings 8:27. Jesus calls the temple 'My Father's house' in John 2:16 and speaks of the temple of His body in John 2:21, and in John 14 He speaks of the Father's house with many rooms. The correspondence is that God lives with His people. The escalation is that the house is now the person of Christ and the community that is in Him, 1 Corinthians 6:19. The type falls short because the tent and the temple were places God's glory visited, while the new house is a people God lives in.

typology.type: The way barred at Eden and the curtain, Genesis 3:24
typology.fulfillment: After the fall God stationed cherubim and a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life, and later the tabernacle was divided by a curtain that kept the people from the Most Holy Place. Jesus says He is the way to the Father, and Hebrews 10:19 and 20 says He opened 'a new and living way' through the curtain of His body. The correspondence is the closed road and the opened one. The escalation is that the road is not merely unbarred but is a person who walks it with His people. The type falls short in that Eden was a place, while the new way is a relationship and a person.

typology.type: The God who goes ahead to find a camp, Deuteronomy 1:33
typology.fulfillment: Moses reminded Israel that the LORD 'went before you on the journey, in the fire by night and in the cloud by day, to seek out a place for you to camp and to show you the road to travel.' Jesus tells His disciples that He goes to prepare a place for them. The correspondence is of a leader who goes ahead to make ready. The escalation is that He goes ahead through death and returns to bring them to Himself, and that the place He prepares is the Father's own house. The type falls short because Israel's camps were temporary and the cloud led to a land that could be lost.

typology.type: Moses' farewell and the succession of Joshua, Deuteronomy 31:6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Before he died Moses told the people not to fear, because the LORD would go with them and would not leave them, and he commissioned Joshua to lead them in. The farewell speech of Jesus has the same shape: a departing leader, a frightened people, a promise of God's presence and a successor. The escalation is that the successor is not a man but the Spirit of truth, and the promise 'I will not leave you as orphans' is fulfilled in the presence of God Himself. The type falls short because Joshua was a mortal who also died, while the Spirit stays forever, verse 16.

study.christ:
The chapter makes Christ the answer to Thomas's honest question. Thomas says he does not know the way, and Jesus does not give directions. He gives Himself. The way is a person, so that to be on the road is to be in relationship with Him. This means that no one has to find some separate route to the Father and then come back to ask Jesus' leave. The Son is the road, and the Father is at the end of it.

He is also the full revelation of the Father. 'Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father,' verse 9, is the counterpart to John 1:18, 'No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known.' Colossians 1:15 and Hebrews 1:3 say the same in the language of image and representation. This is not a claim that the Father and Son are the same person. Jesus says in verse 10 that He is in the Father and the Father in Him, and in verse 28 that the Father is greater, so that the unity is one of a mutual indwelling between two persons.

The works of Jesus are put forward as evidence. 'Believe on account of the works themselves,' verse 11. The signs of John 2 to 11 are not isolated wonders but the Father at work in the Son, and so the believer is invited to look back and read them as a testimony to who He is. Jesus also stands as the one who prays and sends. 'I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate,' verse 16, and the Spirit comes in His name, verse 26. He is the one to whom the Spirit points, and the one by whom the Spirit is given.

Finally, He is the one who gives peace. 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you,' verse 27, is not a wish but a gift, and the cost of the gift is the cross, which is only hours away. Paul says that, 'since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1. The man who is troubled in spirit in 12:27 hands on a peace that has been won in advance. And His going to the Father is not a loss but a gain, because it is by going that He sends the Spirit, as John 16:7 says.

The chapter keeps the Christ of the cross and the Christ of glory together. The prince of this world is coming, and he has no claim on Him, verse 30, and He goes out to meet him because He loves the Father, verse 31. The way, the truth and the life is also the obedient Son who walks to the cross.
study.god:
More than any other chapter of the Gospel, John 14 shows the Trinity in the setting of daily trust. The Father has a house with many rooms. The Son goes to prepare a place, speaks the Father's words and does the Father's works. The Spirit is sent by the Father in the Son's name, verse 26, and asked of the Father by the Son, verse 16. Three persons are named, they act together, and none is reduced to the others. Yet the chapter never explains the Trinity in abstract terms. It shows the Father, Son and Spirit giving themselves to a handful of frightened people.

The God of this chapter is a God who comes to dwell. The Father and Son come to the believer and make a home, verse 23, and the Spirit abides in the believer, verse 17. This ties back to the whole of the Old Testament, where God is the one who walks among His people, Leviticus 26:11 and 12, and who says 'I am coming to dwell among you,' Zechariah 2:10. The unapproachable God of the Law becomes the God who is closer than the people who sit beside His disciples.

There is a real tension in verse 28. Jesus says 'the Father is greater than I,' and a few have used the verse to deny His deity. The church has long read it in the setting of the incarnation. The Son has taken the place of a servant, as Philippians 2:7 says, and He speaks as one sent, so that in His role as the sent one the Father is greater, while in nature He is one with the Father, John 10:30. The verse is not an argument against His deity but a statement about the order of the mission.

The chapter also shows God as a giver of peace and a teacher. The Spirit will 'teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you,' verse 26, which guarantees that what Jesus taught will be faithfully remembered and applied. The God revealed here does not leave His people with a book alone but with a living teacher. His peace is a state of wholeness grounded in the Father's care, and Isaiah 26:3 already spoke of it as the keeping of those who trust in Him.

For worship, this means that prayer goes to the Father, in the Son's name, by the Spirit's help. Romans 8:15 and 16 shows the result: believers cry 'Abba, Father,' and the Spirit testifies with their spirit that they are God's children. The chapter teaches the church to pray as a family at home, not as supplicants outside the door.

crossReferences.note: The prologue's version of verse 9. No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is at the Father's side, has made Him known. Philip's request to see the Father is answered by the fact that the Son is the only one who has seen Him and the only way He is known. The two verses frame the Gospel with the same claim.

'Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth.' The psalmist joins the way and the truth, and Jesus joins them in a person. The prayer asks for what the Gospel says has now been given: a way to walk and a truth to walk in, and a Teacher who is the way and the truth.

The way of verse 6 explained in terms of the temple. Believers have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way through the curtain of His body. It shows how the exclusive claim is also an open door, and how the road to the Father runs through His death.

God stationed cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life. The long closing of the road to God begins here, and John 14:6 is the announcement that it has been reopened. It makes the way of Jesus not a new religious idea but the reversal of the exile from Eden.

Peter, filled with the Spirit, states the exclusive claim in public. 'Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.' The apostles did not soften what Jesus said in the upper room; they preached it, and paid for it, in the same city.

Paul calls the Son 'the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation.' It explains verse 9, 'Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father.' The invisible God is made visible in the Son, who is also the one through whom all things were made, so that the revelation is grounded in His place in creation.

The Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the one who lives in believers, and through Him the Father and Son are present. It shows what Jesus meant when He said the Spirit would be in them and that He would come to them. The indwelling is the way Christ is with His people until the end.

God promised a new heart and His own Spirit within His people so that they would walk in His ways. John 14 announces that the promise is about to be kept. The Spirit who will be in the disciples is the Spirit that Ezekiel foresaw, and the keeping of Jesus' word is the fruit of that new heart.

Moses reassured Israel before his death that the LORD goes with them and will never leave them. The farewell of Jesus draws on the same pattern, and shows that the pattern was a shadow. Moses could promise God's presence, while Jesus can promise that the presence will dwell in them.

'The dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.' The Father's house of John 14:2 and the home made with believers in 14:23 come together in the city where God lives with His people. It is the end of the chapter's promise and the end of the story.

The Spirit's work is unfolded further. He convicts the world, guides the disciples into all truth, and glorifies Jesus by taking from what is His. The promise of John 14:26 that the Spirit will teach and remind is given its fuller shape here, and the Spirit's ministry is tied again to the Father and the Son.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture can be told as a story of a lost home. The first couple walked with God in a garden and were driven east, and everything afterward is a long road back. Abraham journeyed toward a city whose builder is God, Israel followed a pillar toward a promised rest, and the temple was built as a place where heaven and earth met. Each is a partial answer to the question Thomas asks in a few words, how can we know the way?

John 14 answers that the way back has been found and that it is a person. Jesus does not point at a path; He goes ahead through death to prepare a place, and He will bring His people to it. He is the one in whom God and humanity meet, and the one who bears the exile to its end. The cherubim at the garden gate and the curtain before the Most Holy Place are the signs of what He removes.

The chapter also places the Spirit at the centre of the redeemed life. The promise runs from Ezekiel's new heart to Joel's outpouring to Pentecost, and the Spirit is the one who makes the home of verse 23 a present reality. So the story of redemption is not only about what Christ did at the cross but about the God who comes to live in those He has brought home. The distance between the Creator and His creatures is closed from both ends.

The story ends where this chapter points. In Revelation 21:3 the dwelling place of God is with man, and in the new creation the exile is over. The first Adam was sent out of the garden to the east, and the last Adam brings His people into the Father's house. What Thomas could not see in the upper room, a road leading home, the redeemed will walk together, with the Father, the Son and the Spirit at the end of it and beside them all the way.

quiz.q: How does Jesus comfort His troubled disciples at the start of the chapter?

options.text: He promises to prepare a place for them in the Father's house and to come back for them.
options.note: Verses 1 to 3 ground their comfort in His preparing a place and returning.

options.text: He simply tells them not to worry, since worry changes nothing.
options.note: He does say let not your hearts be troubled, but the comfort rests on the prepared place and His return, not positive thinking.

options.text: He assures them He will never leave in the first place.
options.note: He is indeed going away, but promises to return and prepare a place.

options.text: He calls them to trust God and Him amid their fear.
options.note: True, He calls for faith, but the specific comfort is the promise of a prepared place and His return.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by I am the way, the truth, and the life?

options.text: He is Himself the only access to the Father, His true revelation, and the source of life.
options.note: Verse 6 makes Him the exclusive way, the truth, and the life, through whom alone we come to the Father.

options.text: He is one good path among many to God.
options.note: He says no one comes to the Father except through Him, not one path among many.

options.text: He points people toward the way, truth, and life.
options.note: He is not merely a signpost; He is the way, the truth, and the life in person.

options.text: He is the only way to the Father.
options.note: True, but it omits that He is also the truth and the life, the full claim of the verse.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say to Philip's request to see the Father?

options.text: Anyone who has seen Jesus has seen the Father, for He is in the Father and the Father in Him.
options.note: Verses 9 to 11 reveal that the Son perfectly displays the Father.

options.text: No one can ever know what the Father is like.
options.note: The opposite; the Father is truly seen in the Son.

options.text: The Father will be shown only after Jesus dies.
options.note: The Father is already seen in Jesus now; Philip has been looking at Him all along.

options.text: To know the Father, keep looking to Jesus.
options.note: True in direction, but it softens the striking claim that seeing Jesus is seeing the Father.

quiz.q: What does Jesus promise about the Advocate, the Holy Spirit?

options.text: The Father will give another Advocate to be with them forever and to live in them.
options.note: Verses 16 and 17 promise the abiding, indwelling Spirit.

options.text: The Spirit will come only briefly and then leave.
options.note: The Spirit is given to be with them forever, not briefly.

options.text: The Spirit will replace Jesus with a lesser presence.
options.note: The Spirit is another Advocate of the same kind, continuing Jesus' presence, not a lesser substitute.

options.text: The Spirit will teach them and remind them of Jesus' words.
options.note: True, verse 26, but it omits the central promise that the Spirit will be with and in them forever.

quiz.q: What kind of peace does Jesus leave with His disciples?

options.text: His own peace, not as the world gives, so their hearts need not be troubled or afraid.
options.note: Verse 27 contrasts His peace with the world's and calms their fear.

options.text: A calm that comes from their circumstances improving.
options.note: His peace does not depend on easier circumstances; He gives it even as trouble remains, unlike the world's peace.

options.text: The same fragile peace the world offers.
options.note: He explicitly says He does not give as the world gives.

options.text: A peace that steadies them against fear.
options.note: True, but it omits that it is His own peace, unlike anything the world can give.

questions: Jesus met troubled hearts with the promise of a prepared place. When your heart is troubled, where do you turn for comfort, and how might His promise steady you?
Jesus claims to be the only way to the Father. How do you respond to that exclusivity, and how is it actually good news for a world seeking God?
To see Jesus is to see the Father. When you picture God, how closely does that picture match the Jesus of the Gospels?
Jesus said love for Him shows itself in keeping His word. Where is your love for Christ being tested by a command you find hard to obey?
Jesus gives a peace unlike the world's. In what situation do you most need to receive His peace rather than the fragile calm the world offers?

translationNotes.note: Many rooms; the BSB footnote offers an alternate reading of the verse. The image is of ample room in the Father's house for all Jesus' people.
Advocate renders parakletos; the BSB footnote gives Comforter, Helper, or Counselor. The word means one called alongside to help, and applies to the Spirit here and in verse 26.
He abides with you and will be in you; the BSB footnote notes a variant reading is in you. The promise moves from the Spirit's present company to His future indwelling.
The Father is greater than I speaks of the Son's submitted role in His mission, not inferiority of nature, since John elsewhere affirms His oneness with the Father.
